title: Euler's Theorem
short: If gcd(a, n) = 1, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n); use it to find the last digits of huge powers.
trouble: Students reduce the exponent mod n instead of mod φ(n), or use the theorem when gcd(a, n) > 1.

blocks.html: Fermat's theorem shrinks exponents for a prime modulus. Euler found the version for any modulus: replace $p - 1$ by $\varphi(n)$, the number of units. It is the theorem that makes RSA work.

Euler's theorem. If $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, then $$a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}.$$ For a prime, $\varphi(p) = p - 1$ and this is Fermat's theorem. As before, exponents may be reduced mod $\varphi(n)$: if $e \equiv r \pmod{\varphi(n)}$, then $a^{e} \equiv a^{r}$.

Copy Fermat's proof, using only the units. Let $u_1, \dots, u_{\varphi(n)}$ be the units mod $n$. Multiplying each by $a$ (itself a unit) gives units again, all different (cancel $a$ with its inverse), so $au_1, \dots, au_{\varphi(n)}$ are the same units in a new order. Multiply everything: $$a^{\varphi(n)} \, u_1 \cdots u_{\varphi(n)} \equiv u_1 \cdots u_{\varphi(n)} \pmod{n}.$$ The product of units is a unit, so it cancels.

blocks.name: nt-powers
blocks.cap: The last digit of a power of 7 cycles through 7, 9, 3, 1, a period of $\varphi(10) = 4$. So the last digit of $7^{222}$ is the last digit of $7^{2}$, since $222 = 4 \cdot 55 + 2$.

blocks.title: Last two digits
blocks.q: Find the last two digits of $3^{1000}$.

blocks.title: An exponent tower
steps: The exponent is $3^{3} = 27$. Reduce it mod $\varphi(10) = 4$: $27 \equiv 3$.

blocks.title: Inverses from Euler
steps: $5 \cdot 5^{\varphi(12) - 1} = 5^{\varphi(12)} \equiv 1$, so $5^{-1} \equiv 5^{\varphi(12) - 1} = 5^{3}$. In general $a^{-1} \equiv a^{\varphi(n) - 1}$ for a unit $a$.

blocks.html: Reducing the exponent mod $n$ instead of mod $\varphi(n)$, or using the theorem when $\gcd(a, n) > 1$. Mod 10, $2^{\varphi(10)} = 2^{4} = 16 \equiv 6$, not 1: the powers of 2 never reach 1 mod 10, because 2 is not a unit. When $\gcd(a, n) > 1$, factor $n$ and use the CRT, or look for the repeating pattern directly.

This theorem is the engine of RSA. If $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}$, then $ed = 1 + k\varphi(n)$, and for every unit $m$, $(m^{e})^{d} = m \cdot (m^{\varphi(n)})^{k} \equiv m$. Raising to the power $e$ scrambles $m$; raising to the power $d$ unscrambles it.
$\varphi(n)$ is a period, not always the shortest one. Mod 15, $\varphi(15) = 8$, yet $2^{4} = 16 \equiv 1$ already. The shortest period is the order of $a$, which always divides $\varphi(n)$.
If $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, then $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, so reduce exponents mod $\varphi(n)$. Check the gcd first.
